hooks.text: Spacecraft never dodge giant rocks while crossing the asteroid belt.
Why is the asteroid belt so empty that rocks are 600,000 miles apart?
The average distance between asteroids in the belt is six hundred thousand miles.

title: The Lonely Reality of the Asteroid Belt
description: Discover why the asteroid belt is a vast, empty desert rather than the crowded obstacle course shown in movies.

beats.text: Spacecraft never dodge giant rocks while crossing the asteroid belt.
beats.visual: NASA artist's concept of a spacecraft traversing a sparse asteroid belt, 1972

beats.text: On January 1, 1801, astronomer Giuseppe Piazzi discovered the first fragment, Ceres, while hunting for a missing planet.
beats.visual: Portrait of Giuseppe Piazzi, astronomer painting

beats.text: An informal group called the Celestial Police formed to search for this predicted missing world.
beats.visual: Diagram of the Titius-Bode Law, solar system orbits

beats.text: Instead of a single planet, they found a vast graveyard of planetesimals prevented from merging by Jupiter's massive gravity.
beats.visual: Diagram of the Solar System showing the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter

beats.text: The average distance between these space rocks is about 600,000 miles, making the belt an extreme cosmic desert.
beats.visual: Dwarf planet Ceres as seen by Dawn spacecraft, 2015

beats.text: Spacecraft safely cruise through because the probability of hitting an asteroid is less than one in a billion.
beats.visual: Pioneer 10 spacecraft illustration in outer space
